desc:
A collection of integers (duplicates allowed) starts empty and is changed by a list of operations. ops[i] = [type, x]:

  • type = 1: insert the value x;
  • type = 2: delete one occurrence of the value x (it is guaranteed to be present).

The collection is never empty after any operation. After each operation, report twice the median of the collection (the middle value for an odd size, the sum of the two middle values for an even size).

ops = [[1,5], [1,2], [1,8], [2,2], [1,1]]
{5}       -> 10
{2,5}     -> 7
{2,5,8}   -> 10
delete 2: {5,8}   -> 13
insert 1: {1,5,8} -> 10
answer = [10, 7, 10, 13, 10]
constraints: A deletion always names a value that is currently present
The collection is non-empty after every operation
hints: Two heaps handle insertions nicely. What makes a deletion hard is that the value may be buried deep inside one of the heaps.
You can tell which heap holds x: if x is at most the root of the lower half (after cleaning), it is in the lower heap, otherwise in the upper heap.
Do not search for it. Record a pending deletion for that heap (a counter per value), shrink that heap's live size, rebalance, and discard stale entries only when they reach the top.
editorial: Keep a max-heap lo for the smaller half and a min-heap hi for the larger half, with live sizes tracked separately from the physical heap sizes. Every value in lo is at most every value in hi, so a value x that is at most the live root of lo must live in lo; otherwise it lives in hi. (If x equals the root it is safe to take it from lo.)

A deletion records x in a per-heap “pending removal” counter and reduces that heap's live size. Whenever a root is needed, entries at the top whose value has a pending removal are popped and the counter is decremented. After the size change, the usual rebalance (move a root across until lo has the same number of live elements as hi or one more) restores the invariant.

Keeping the pending counters separate for the two heaps matters: equal values can sit in both heaps, and a removal must only consume entries from the heap it was assigned to. Each operation is O(log n) amortised, giving O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
